content: Sleep positioning systems are sometimes prescribed for children with cerebral palsy to help reduce or prevent hip migration, alleviate pain, and improve sleep quality. Sleep disturbances are common in children with developmental disabilities and can also affect the sleep of their caregivers. Since these systems can be expensive, clear guidance is necessary to support decisions regarding their use. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether commercially available sleep positioning systems, compared to usual care, are effective in reducing or preventing hip migration in children with cerebral palsy. Any potential negative effects of these systems on hip migration were also considered. Secondary objectives included evaluating the impact of sleep positioning systems on the number or frequency of hip problems, sleep patterns and quality, the quality of life of the child and their family, pain levels, and physical functioning. Additionally, the review aimed to identify any adverse effects associated with the use of these systems. In December 2014, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as 13 other databases and two trial registries. No restrictions were applied regarding the date of publication, language, publication status, or study design. References were checked, manufacturers and authors were contacted for relevant literature, and internet searches were performed using Google. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated whole-body sleep positioning systems for children and adolescents (up to 18 years of age) with cerebral palsy. Two independent reviewers screened the search results against pre-determined inclusion criteria and assessed the quality of eligible studies. Parent caregivers of children with neurodisabilities contributed to the review by suggesting the topic, refining the research objectives, interpreting the findings, and reviewing the plain language summary. No randomized controlled trials were identified that evaluated the effectiveness of sleep positioning systems in reducing or preventing hip migration. However, two randomized cross-over trials met the inclusion criteria for secondary objectives related to sleep quality and pain. These studies involved a total of 21 children and provided very low-quality evidence. Neither study found significant differences in sleep patterns or sleep quality between children using sleep positioning systems and those not using them. Similarly, one study involving 11 children found no significant differences in pain levels. Both studies were small, involved children who were already established users of sleep positioning systems, and were judged to have a high risk of bias. No eligible trials were found that addressed other secondary objectives, such as the number or frequency of hip problems, the quality of life of the child and their family, physical functioning, or adverse effects. In conclusion, no randomized trials were identified that evaluated the effectiveness of sleep positioning systems in reducing or preventing hip migration in children with cerebral palsy. Additionally, no trials were found that assessed their impact on the number or frequency of hip problems, quality of life, or physical functioning. Limited data from two small trials suggested no significant differences in sleep quality or pain when using sleep positioning systems. To guide clinical decision-making and the prescription of these systems, more rigorous research is needed to evaluate their effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and potential adverse effects.
